transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
I've been struggling a lot with constantly feeling restless and fidgeting. I just can't seem to sit still or keep my hands and feet quiet, and it's really starting to bother me.
Do you also have trouble paying attention, staying organized, or finishing tasks, or is it mainly the restlessness and fidgeting?

It’s actually both. I constantly fidget, tap my hands or feet, and squirm in my seat, but I also really struggle to organize my tasks and daily activities. On top of that, I get easily distracted by things going on around me or even just my own unrelated thoughts.
Have these attention and restlessness symptoms been present since childhood, before age 12?

Yes, they definitely have. Looking back, I can remember struggling with being restless and disorganized since elementary school, well before I turned 12. It feels like it's always been an issue for me.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)], but the patient now endorses clear inattentive symptoms in addition to hyperactivity/impulsivity: difficulty organizing tasks, distractibility, and longstanding problems since childhood. That makes the predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation unlikely and leaves ADHD combined presentation as the best fit.

inference_history.note: No previous candidates were provided, so this is the initial differential based on the report of constant restlessness and fidgeting. ADHD remains possible because motor restlessness and difficulty sitting still can reflect hyperactivity/impulsivity, especially if longstanding. Generalized Anxiety Disorder is also possible because restlessness is a common anxiety symptom. Adjustment Disorder is included as a broader possibility if these symptoms began after a recent stressor. Predominantly inattentive ADHD is not supported yet because no inattention symptoms were described, and mood or psychotic disorders are not suggested by the current transcript.

inference_history.note: Previously the candidates included ADHD combined, ADHD predominantly hyperactive/impulsive, generalized anxiety disorder, and adjustment disorder. The patient now endorses both prominent hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms (fidgeting, squirming, inability to sit still) and inattentive symptoms (difficulty organizing tasks, distractibility), which supports ADHD combined presentation. Generalized anxiety disorder is less likely because the core complaint is not excessive worry/tension but a longstanding pattern of inattention and hyperactivity. Adjustment disorder is also less likely because no clear recent stressor or time-limited reaction has been described. ADHD predominantly hyperactive/impulsive remains possible, but the inattentive symptoms make combined presentation more likely.
